# Lab6PKG

<!-- badges: start -->
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/kanneb/Lab6PKG/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/kanneb/Lab6PKG/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)
<!-- badges: end -->

Lab6PKG solves the knapsack problem with three methods: brute force search, dynamic programming and a greedy heuristic. The brute force search can also run in C++ with Rcpp.

## Installation

Install from GitHub. Set the option first if you also want the vignette:

``` r
# install.packages("pak")
options(pkg.build_vignettes = TRUE)
pak::pak("kanneb/Lab6PKG")
```

## Examples

The data is generated as following. `x` needs a weight column `w` and a value column `v`, and `W` is the size of the knapsack.

```{r data}
library(Lab6PKG)

suppressWarnings(RNGversion(min(as.character(getRversion()), "3.5.3")))
set.seed(42, kind = "Mersenne-Twister", normal.kind = "Inversion")
n <- 2000
knapsack_objects <- data.frame(
  w = sample(1:4000, size = n, replace = TRUE),
  v = runif(n = n, 0, 10000)
)
```

Brute force search goes through all combinations, so keep `n` small. Use `fast = TRUE` to run the search in C++:

```{r brute}
brute_force_knapsack(x = knapsack_objects[1:8, ], W = 3500)
brute_force_knapsack(x = knapsack_objects[1:8, ], W = 3500, fast = TRUE)
```

Dynamic programming gives the exact answer and works with larger `n`, as long as the weights are integers:

```{r dynamic}
knapsack_dynamic(x = knapsack_objects[1:500, ], W = 3500)
```

The greedy heuristic is the fastest but only approximate:

```{r greedy}
greedy_knapsack(x = knapsack_objects[1:800, ], W = 3500)
```

All functions return a list with the total `value` and the row numbers in `elements`.

## More

The vignette contains the lab report with timings and answers to the questions:

``` r
browseVignettes("Lab6PKG")
```
